Now let me compile everything into a verse-by-verse commentary.

---

# Proverbs 5 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter is the eighth admonitory discourse in Proverbs: a warning against adultery coupled with a commendation of faithful marriage. The Pulpit Commentary divides it into three sections: (1) an appeal for attention because of the deceptive allure of the adulteress (vv.1–6); (2) the main didactic section: warnings against the adulteress (vv.7–14) and the positive exhortation to marital fidelity (vv.15–20); (3) an epilogue emphasizing divine accountability (vv.21–23). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

Gill summarises: "The general instruction of this chapter is to avoid whoredom, and make use of lawful marriage, and keep to that." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

Constable notes that chapters 5–7 each deal with sexual sin from a different angle: chapter 5 = eventual disappointment; chapter 6 = gradual destruction; chapter 7 = ultimate death. (Search result from Constable's Expository Notes)

---

## v. 1 — "My son, pay attention to my wisdom; incline your ear to my insight"

**Traditional Reading:** Solomon opens with an urgent, personal appeal. The teacher is not offering abstract philosophy but wisdom gained through costly experience (perhaps alluding to Solomon's own disastrous marriages — 1 Kings 11). "Bow down thine ear" pictures bending the ear toward the speaker, listening with intense concentration. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

**Gill:** This is not worldly wisdom but "spiritual and evangelical wisdom; such as one that is greater than Solomon has in him, even Christ." The Gospel and its doctrines are "the wisdom of God in a mystery" (1 Cor 2:7). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

**Precept Austin:** Precept Austin emphasises that verbs in this section are "commands, not suggestions." Solomon repeatedly calls for attention in Proverbs 5–7, knowing the power of sexual sin. Wisdom (chokmah) is "the ability to see something from God's viewpoint." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-5-commentary)

**Bridges (Anglican/Evangelical):** "Perhaps painful experience (1 Kings 11:1-8; Ecclesiastes 7:26) had given the wise man wisdom and understanding. Therefore attend to it with fear and trembling." (Search result from Bridges' Commentary)

---

## v. 2 — "that you may maintain discretion and your lips may preserve knowledge"

**Traditional Reading:** Paying attention to wisdom has two practical results: (a) the son will "maintain discretion" — i.e. guard good judgment, control his thoughts, and form prudent resolutions; (b) his lips will "preserve knowledge," speaking only what is consistent with the knowledge of God and never falling into seductive or foolish speech. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

**Garner-Howes (Baptist):** The son is to "take care to act with discretion and to speak consistent with the knowledge or learning he has acquired." (Search result from Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary)

**Constable (Evangelical):** "The lips of the youth (v. 2) contrast with those of the seductress (v. 3). Knowing what is right and being able to articulate that with one's lips is really a protection against the power of the seductress's speech." (Search result from Constable's Expository Notes)

**Precept Austin:** Bridges is quoted: "Man's own strength, the restraint of education or self-discipline, is powerless, as the green withes to bind the giant (Judges 16:9). Engrafted wisdom is the only effectual safeguard." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-5-commentary)

---

## v. 3 — "Though the lips of the forbidden woman drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil"

**Traditional Reading:** The "strange woman" (zarah) is a harlot or adulteress — either a foreigner, or more likely the wife of another man (cf. Proverbs 7:19), making her an adulteress. Her words are as attractive as honey dripping from the comb and as smooth as olive oil. The image is of flattery and seductive speech — the first steps toward sin are almost always through words. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Ellicott:** Notes that the phrase "smoother than oil" recalls David's experience with Ahithophel (Psalm 55:21) — the treachery of a trusted friend whose words were soft but intentions deadly. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Gill:** "The kisses of whose lips, her confabulations and songs, are as pleasing to the carnal senses of men as honey is sweet to the taste." He also applies this allegorically to the "whore of Rome" drawing people into idolatry "by the blandishments of pomp and grandeur." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

**Enduring Word (Guzik, charismatic/Pentecostal):** The honey and oil represent "the temptations of immorality." The figures of lips and mouth refer both to "the words an immoral woman may use in her enticements, and to her alluring kisses." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

---

## v. 4 — "in the end she is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a double-edged sword"

**Traditional Reading:** The contrast is vivid: honey becomes bitterness, smooth oil becomes a cutting blade. "Wormwood" (laanah, Artemisia absinthium) was regarded in the ancient Near East as both intensely bitter and poisonous (cf. Deuteronomy 29:18; Revelation 8:11). The "end" refers not only to the woman's own fate but to what her victims experience — remorse, anguish of heart, and death. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

**Ellicott:** Compares the two-edged sword imagery to Revelation 10:10, where the message was "sweet as honey in the mouth" but made the belly bitter — through tribulation one enters the kingdom. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Gill:** "Her end is bitter as wormwood" is opposed to the honeycomb of v.3 — loss of credit, substance, health, remorse of conscience, fear of death both corporeal and eternal. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

**Garner-Howes (Baptist):** "It is a sin upon which God has pronounced judgment, Ecclesiastes 7:26; Hebrews 13:4." (Search result from Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary)

---

## v. 5 — "Her feet go down to death; her steps lead straight to Sheol"

**Traditional Reading:** The harlot's path descends inevitably toward death and the grave (Sheol). Not merely physical death, but death as punishment. The second line intensifies the first: the descent becomes a firm grip — "her steps take hold on hell" (KJV). Ellicott: "They lead straight to it." The same description appears in Proverbs 2:18; 7:27; 9:18. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

**Gill:** Her ways always lead to eternal death "if grace prevent not." She not only goes to hell herself but brings all her followers there. He also applies it to antichrist: "the whore of Rome…she goes herself, and hither she brings all that follow her idolatrous practices." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

**Ligonier (Reformed):** Notes that in the original context this likely referenced the death penalty for adultery in ancient Israel (Leviticus 20:10), but even where adultery is not a capital crime, "adultery still destroys life. It breaks up families and marriages. It can spread disease." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/trap-adultery)

---

## v. 6 — "She does not consider the path of life; she does not know that her ways are unstable"

**Traditional Reading — a translation crux:** The KJV renders "Lest thou shouldest ponder the path of life, her ways are moveable, that thou canst not know them." Most modern translations and commentators (Ellicott, Pulpit, Delitzsch) take the verse as a series of statements about the woman herself: "She walks not in the path of life; her ways fluctuate; she knows not." The Pulpit Commentary explains that the Hebrew pen is unique here in the sense of "not" (rather than "lest"). The picture is of "the reckless career of a vicious woman, who at last dares not think whither her steps are leading her, but as it were with eyes shut, totters on till she falls to rise no more." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

**Garner-Howes (Baptist):** Takes the KJV approach: "The seductress frequently changes her allurements to divert the prospective partner's attention and thus prevent his pondering the evils of the contemplated sin." (Search result from Garner-Howes)

**Gill (older Baptist):** "She appears in different shapes; changes her dress and habitation; makes use of a thousand arts to ensnare men…she leads them into various mazes and labyrinths of sin, till they have lost all sense of religion, and sight of the path of life." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

---

## v. 7 — "So now, my sons, listen to me, and do not turn aside from the words of my mouth"

**Traditional Reading:** The plural "my sons" (children) marks a fresh start in the discourse. The Pulpit Commentary notes that though the address is to all, the singular is immediately resumed, "that each individually is to apply it to himself." The teacher has finished describing the harlot's character; now he amplifies the warning with concrete consequences. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

**Gill:** Since the character and end of the adulterous woman have been laid out, "those that are young in years, and liable to be ensnared by her, should hear what Solomon, or Christ, here says." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** "We sense the serious nature of Solomon's appeal. Perhaps he understood how adultery brought disaster to his father, King David (2 Samuel 11)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

---

## v. 8 — "Keep your path far from her; do not go near the door of her house"

**Traditional Reading:** The prime defence is distance — not testing one's resistance but fleeing. This is the same counsel Paul gives: "Flee fornication" (1 Corinthians 6:18) and "Flee youthful lusts" (2 Timothy 2:22). The Pulpit Commentary cites the old proverb: "He that would no evil do / Must do nothing that 'longeth thereto." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

**Ellicott:** "The great safeguard in such temptations, as all moralists with one mouth advise, is flight." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** Applies this beyond physical presence: "We must remove our way far from her not only in presence, but also in heart and mind. We must put away the pornography and enticements common to our day." Kidner is quoted: "This practical, if seemingly unheroic, advice…could mean, in terms of detailed decision, e.g. 'change your job', 'change your newspaper', 'break with that set of friends.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Bridges (Anglican/Evangelical):** "To thrust ourselves into temptation, is to throw ourselves out of God's protection." (Search result from Bridges' Commentary)

---

## v. 9 — "lest you concede your vigor to others, and your years to one who is cruel"

**Traditional Reading:** "Honour" (Hebrew hod) is better rendered "freshness, vigour" — the bloom and beauty of youth. "Years" refers to the best, most vigorous years of life. These are surrendered to "the cruel one" — which Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary interpret either as the temptress herself (cruel, pitiless), her husband (who will deal mercilessly with the adulterer), or her associates who live off the ruined youth. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

**Gill:** The "cruel" may be "the jealous husband of the adulterous woman, who will not spare the adulterer when taken by him; or her brethren, her relations and friends; or her other gallants…or the civil magistrate." Jarchi interpreted it of "the prince of hell, the devil." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

---

## v. 10 — "lest strangers feast on your wealth, and your labors enrich the house of a foreigner"

**Traditional Reading:** The adulterer's wealth and the fruit of his toil end up in the hands of "strangers" — the harlot, her household, and her associates. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew koakh ("wealth") derives from a root meaning "strength" — the concrete product of one's strength when brought into action. What was earned by sweat ends up in a stranger's house. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm)

**Gill:** "Wealth gotten by hard labour, with toil and sweat, grief and trouble…and yet, after all, not enjoyed by himself and his lawful wife and children, but by the strange woman and her accomplices, and spent in maintaining whores, bawds, and bastards." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** Cites Waltke: "Although sexual immorality today may not lead to slavery, it still leads to alimony, child support, broken homes, hurt, jealousy, lonely people, and venereal disease." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

---

## v. 11 — "At the end of your life you will groan when your flesh and your body are spent"

**Traditional Reading:** Physical ruin follows financial ruin. The word "groan" (naham) means to roar or growl like a lion — expressing extreme distress. The "flesh and body consumed" points to venereal diseases that waste the body, or simply the toll that a double life of sin takes on health. Ellicott: "Ruin of health has followed ruin of property." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Precept Austin (Mark Copeland outline):** Lists this under "The Price of Adultery — It Costs Your Physical Health," noting bacterial STDs (chlamydia, syphilis, gonorrhea) and viral STDs (herpes, Hepatitis B, AIDS). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-5-commentary)

**Matthew Poole (cited by Enduring Word):** The body is "consumed by those manifold diseases which filthy and inordinate lusts bring upon the body, of which physicians give a very large and sad catalogue." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

---

## vv. 12–13 — "and you will say, 'How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof! I did not listen to the voice of my teachers or incline my ear to my mentors.'"

**Traditional Reading:** The final agony is remorse — too late. Ellicott: "The last stage of misery is the remorse which comes too late. (Comp. Matthew 25:30.)" The ruined man recalls with bitterness the instructions he rejected from parents, teachers, and ministers. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Debate — genuine or false repentance?** Matthew Poole thought these were not words of true repentance — only grief over consequences, not over the sin itself. John Trapp thought it *could* describe true, though late, repentance. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Gill:** "He says, as wondering at his stupidity, folly, and madness, that he should hate and abhor that which was so much his interest to have observed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

**Precept Austin (Copeland):** "It Costs Your Mental Health…Your conscience can eat away at your peace of mind." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-5-commentary)

---

## v. 14 — "I am on the brink of utter ruin in the midst of the whole assembly"

**Traditional Reading:** Ellicott gives two interpretations: (1) "I had almost fallen into every sin: I was so infatuated that I might have committed any sin, and that openly before all" — the offender shudders to think how much worse it might have been; (2) "I might have been visited with extremest punishment at the hands of the congregation, death by stoning (Leviticus 20:10; John 8:5)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Garner-Howes (Baptist):** Lists this as the fifth consequence: "Public disgrace, scandal." (Search result from Garner-Howes)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** "What the adulterer thought would remain secret was exposed. He entered his sin thinking, no one will ever find out." Quotes Trapp: "No unclean person can have any assurance that his sin shall always be kept secret, no, not in this life." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Ligonier (Reformed):** This verse shows adultery "brings shame and disgrace in the covenant community upon those who commit it." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/trap-adultery)

---

## v. 15 — "Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well"

**Traditional Reading:** The imagery shifts to the positive antidote: marital fidelity. The cistern and well are metaphors for one's own wife (cf. Song of Solomon 4:15). As water quenches thirst, so the lawful enjoyments of marriage quench the thirst of lust (cf. 1 Corinthians 7:9). The possessive "your own" is emphatic — the point is exclusive, private satisfaction within marriage. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/5.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Gill:** "As every man formerly had his own cistern for the reception of water for his own use (2 Kings 18:31); so every man should have his own wife, and but one." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** "'Water' in Proverbs 5:15, as in Song of Solomon 5:1, stands for quenching one's sexual thirst." Quotes Clarke: "Be satisfied with thy own wife; and let the wife see that she reverence her husband; and not tempt him by inattention or unkindness to seek elsewhere." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Bridges (Anglican/Evangelical):** "A restless dissatisfaction with our present blessings cherishes the lust for forbidden pleasures. Where contentment is not found at home — drinking out of our own cistern, it will not be found abroad." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_515-23_commentary)

**Precept Austin:** "The best way for a man to avoid sexual misconduct (including indulging in pornography and the fantasizing and self-gratification that naturally accompany this sin) is to (1) have a loving relationship with your Creator and (2) secondly a loving relationship with the wife of your youth. In short, to experience the expulsive power of a new affection!" (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_515-23_commentary)

---

## v. 16 — "Why should your springs flow in the streets, your streams of water in the public squares?"

**Traditional Reading:** The image of water flowing wastefully in public streets contrasts with the private, treasured waters of marriage. The idea is: why should what is precious and intimate (sexual relations) be squandered in the public sphere — with prostitutes or adulteresses? Ellicott interprets "fountains" as offspring: why should a man father children illegitimately who are then dispersed without a true home? (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Constable (Evangelical):** Notes a textual variant: "The Hebrew text favors taking Proverbs 5:16 as a positive statement ('Let your streams…') rather than as a question." Kidner's view: "The influence of the faithful man (His 'springs') become a blessing to others." (Search result from Constable)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** "The best approach seems to be a contrast between private and public. God meant for sex to be enjoyed and celebrated in the privacy of marriage, not in the public or even commercial sphere." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

---

## v. 17 — "Let them be yours alone, never to be shared with strangers"

**Traditional Reading:** The deepest joys of married life are sacred and not to be shared outside the marriage bond. Ellicott: "The deepest joys and sorrows of each heart are sacred, and cannot be shared with others (Proverbs 14:10), and so it is with the various relations of family life also, strangers have no part in them." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Precept Austin:** "The sexual intimacy described in these verses is ultimately relational intimacy, 'never to be shared with strangers' (Pr 5:17; cf. 1 Cor. 7:3–5)." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-5-commentary)

**Garner-Howes (Baptist):** "Fathering illegitimate children violates a fundamental principle of God's plan, 1 Timothy 5:14; Hebrews 13:4." (Search result from Garner-Howes)

---

## v. 18 — "May your fountain be blessed, and may you rejoice in the wife of your youth"

**Traditional Reading:** "Fountain" here refers to the wife (as source of sexual satisfaction) or possibly to the husband's own procreative capacity. "Let thy fountain be blessed" is "as a reward for purity of life, the blessing of a numerous offspring is invoked" (cf. Psalm 128:3). "The wife of thy youth" implies marrying young and staying faithful for life — God's best design. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Solomon alluded to God's plan for marriage, even if he did not follow it himself (1 Kings 11:3)…Solomon's failure in this area shows that if a man is not satisfied with one woman — the wife of his youth — then he will not be satisfied with 1,000 women." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Precept Austin:** Quotes Bridges: "'First — choose thy love; then love thy choice.' Quench thy thirst out of thine own, and lust not after thy neighbour's, well." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_515-23_commentary)

---

## v. 19 — "A loving doe, a graceful fawn — may her breasts satisfy you always; may you be captivated by her love forever"

**Traditional Reading:** The imagery of the deer (hind and roe) draws on Oriental poetry where these animals symbolise grace, beauty, speed, and tender affection. Ellicott notes both animals are "remarkable for their affection to their young." The verse is strikingly erotic — a strong affirmation that sexual delight within marriage is God-given and good. The word rendered "captivated" (or "ravished," KJV) is the Hebrew shagah, which signifies a staggering gait and can mean "be intoxicated always with her love." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** "It is highly important to see sexual delight in marriage as God-given…God created sex not only for reproduction but also for enjoyment, and He didn't put the 'marriage wall' around sex to rob us of pleasure but to increase pleasure and protect it" (citing Wiersbe and Kidner). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Precept Austin:** "Being satisfied with your wife's breasts is as erotic as it sounds (Pr 5:19)…this command places a holy responsibility upon both partners in the marriage." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-5-commentary)

**Constable (Evangelical):** "The erotic language of Proverbs 5:19-20 may be surprising, but it shows that God approves sexual joy in marriage and it is a prophylactic against unfaithfulness (cf. 1 Corinthians 7:5, 9)." (Search result from Constable)

---

## v. 20 — "Why be captivated, my son, by an adulteress, or embrace the bosom of a stranger?"

**Traditional Reading:** The rhetorical question drives home the absurdity of adultery in light of the satisfying provision of marriage just described. If a man has the wife of his youth, why seek the embrace of a stranger? The word "captivated" (shagah — the same root as v.19) creates a deliberate contrast: be intoxicated with your wife's love, not with an adulteress. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Gill:** The consideration of divine omniscience is now brought forward "to deter him from the sin of adultery." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

---

## v. 21 — "For a man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and the LORD examines all his paths"

**Traditional Reading:** A theological anchor: God's omniscience. No sin is hidden. Ellicott: "Another reason for avoiding sin is the certainty of detection by the Judge, whose 'eyes run to and fro through the whole earth' (2 Chronicles 16:9; cf. Psalm 11:4)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** "The closing reminder that God sees all our ways and ponders all our paths cuts through the illusion that hidden sin is excused sin; before God, no transgression is concealed." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Precept Austin (Copeland outline):** Lists this under "Love Your Lord": "God will judge fornicators and adulterers — Hebrews 13:4. When one sins against the Lord, their sins will be exposed — Numbers 32:23." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-5-commentary)

**Garner-Howes (Baptist):** "All the ways of man are known and seen by the LORD. He is aware of all man does or plans." (Search result from Garner-Howes)

---

## v. 22 — "The iniquities of a wicked man entrap him; the cords of his sin entangle him"

**Traditional Reading:** Sin is self-destructive. The sinner is caught in his own snare — a common biblical theme (Psalm 7:15–16; 57:6). Ellicott: "He has sinned so long that he is 'tied and bound,' hand and foot, with the 'chain of his sins,' and cannot get free even had he the wish to do so." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Enduring Word (Guzik):** "Sexual sin — especially the violation of the marriage covenant — is a sin that entraps and destroys. It brings death, not life." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

**Gill:** "His own iniquities shall take the wicked himself…he shall be holden with the cords of his sins." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

---

## v. 23 — "He dies for lack of discipline, led astray by his own great folly"

**Traditional Reading:** "Without instruction" (KJV) is better translated "for lack of discipline" — the sinner dies not because he didn't know better but because he would not control himself. Ellicott: "For want of discipline, because he would not control himself, 'he shall die,' and 'for the greatness of his folly (self-will) he shall go astray,' and 'wander where there is no way' (Job 12:24)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/5.htm)

**Constable (Evangelical):** "People usually do not become unfaithful to their spouses because they do not know better but because they do not choose better." (Search result from Constable)

**Precept Austin:** "Foolishness and a lack of self-discipline lead one away from the path of life." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs-5-commentary)

**Garner-Howes (Baptist):** "The man who yields shall die for lack of self discipline; because of his great folly he is lost, Proverbs 7:22-23." (Search result from Garner-Howes)

---

## Denominational Distinctives

### Reformed (Ligonier)
Emphasises that adultery is not the unforgivable sin — those who repent will be forgiven — but it always has destructive consequences (loss of good name, divorce, children's respect, job). "Though there is hope in forgiveness, adultery brings destruction." The warning is grounded in God's omniscient judgment and the covenant community. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/trap-adultery)

### Baptist
The Garner-Howes commentary is representative of a traditional Baptist approach: straightforward, emphasises the consequences (loss of honour, wealth, health, remorse, public disgrace), and stresses self-discipline and the fear of God. Gill adds a strong anti-Catholic polemic, applying the "strange woman" allegorically to the "whore of Rome." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-5.html)

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik)
Guzik's commentary is practical and application-heavy, emphasising "putting distance" between oneself and temptation in practical terms (changing media habits, job, friends). He stresses that marital faithfulness is "an act of will, not merely feeling" — you choose to be enraptured. The approach is pastorally warm with strong emphasis on the goodness of sexual pleasure within marriage as God's design. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-5/)

### Anglican/Evangelical (Bridges, Ellicott)
Bridges' commentary (19th c. Anglican) is devotionally rich, emphasising the deceitfulness of sin and the necessity of "engrafted wisdom" as the only effectual safeguard. Ellicott is more text-critical and scholarly, attending to translation issues and cross-references. Both share the mainstream Protestant consensus.
